node.title: Total ATP yield from one glucose molecule
node.canonical_question: How many ATP molecules can one glucose molecule produce through aerobic respiration?
node.summary: Complete oxidation of one glucose can yield approximately 30-32 ATP under cellular conditions via glycolysis, Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation.

seeds: Why does the theoretical maximum of ~38 ATP differ from the ~30-32 actually observed in cells?
How is ATP yield split between glycolysis, the Krebs cycle, and oxidative phosphorylation?
Why does anaerobic respiration produce far less ATP than aerobic respiration?
How do NADH and FADH2 each contribute to the final ATP count?
parsed.rendering_md:
Complete aerobic breakdown of one glucose molecule yields approximately **30 to 32 ATP** under real cellular conditions.

Here is how those ATP molecules are generated across the three stages:

| Stage | Net ATP (direct) | Electron carriers produced | ATP equivalent |
|---|---|---|---|
| Glycolysis (cytoplasm) | 2 ATP | 2 NADH | ~3-5 ATP |
| Pyruvate oxidation + Krebs cycle (mitochondrion) | 2 GTP (~2 ATP) | 8 NADH, 2 FADH2 | ~20-22 ATP |
| **Total** | | | **~30-32 ATP** |

Older textbooks often quoted 36-38 ATP. The lower modern figure accounts for the energy cost of shuttling NADH across the inner mitochondrial membrane and the protons consumed by the ATP/ADP translocase.

The bulk of the ATP (roughly 26-28 out of ~30-32) comes from **oxidative phosphorylation** in the mitochondrion, driven by the proton gradient built up by the electron transport chain.
